summary: Lists the numbers assigned for networks, protocols and similar identifiers used on the ARPA Internet at the time. It was one edition in a series of such lists. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 790.

eli5.summary: A phone book for the early internet, saying which number goes with which network or service. Newer editions replaced it.

subtitle: A registry of protocol numbers, port assignments, and network identifiers for the early Internet.

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET grew, hosts needed to assign protocol numbers, TCP/UDP ports, network numbers, and other identifiers, but there was no centralized registry to prevent conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 776 documents the assignments in use as of January 1981, including assigned network numbers (0-42), Internet version numbers (4 bits), Internet protocol numbers (8 bits), TCP and UDP ports (0-255 range shown), and link numbers. Jon Postel at ISI served as the registry administrator.
tldr.outcome: This edition was one in a series of periodic registry snapshots. Later RFCs and the IANA registry system replaced these snapshot documents, but it stands as a historical record of early Internet numbering.

today: RFC 776 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 790 in 1981 and later superseded by the IANA registry system, which maintains authoritative assignments for protocol numbers, port numbers, and other Internet parameters.

sections.title: The Purpose of Number Assignment
sections.content: RFC 776 is a registry of all the numbers assigned for use in ARPANET protocols and networks. It documents the fields in the Internet Protocol (IP), the protocol and port numbers used in TCP and UDP, network addresses, and link identifiers used in the ARPANET Host-to-IMP interface. Assignments were made by Jon Postel at the Information Sciences Institute, who maintained the registry and issued new numbers on request.
sections.eli5: Every computer on a network needs different numbers for its name, its protocols, and its ports. This list kept track of who got which numbers.

sections.title: What Was Registered
sections.content: The RFC covers five main categories. Network numbers occupy an 8-bit field in IP, with entries 0-42 assigned to specific networks (ARPANET, SATNET, UCLNET, MIT, and more) and the rest reserved or unassigned. Internet version numbers are 4 bits, with version 4 assigned to IP and version 5 to ST Datagram Mode. Protocol numbers are 8 bits: protocol 6 is TCP, 17 is UDP, and others cover experimental protocols like Chaos, NVP, and XNET. Port and socket numbers for TCP and UDP are shown in specific ranges: 0-63 for network-wide functions, 64-131 for host-specific functions, and 224-255 for experimental use. Link numbers are 8 bits used in the ARPANET Host-to-IMP interface.
sections.eli5: The document listed which numbers were reserved for IP versions, protocols like TCP and UDP, and port numbers for services like Telnet, mail, and file transfer.

sections.title: A Snapshot in Time
sections.content: This RFC obsoletes nine earlier RFCs and themselves RFCs (770, 762, 758, 755, 750, 739, 604, 503, 433, 349) and several IENs. It was one edition in an ongoing series of registry snapshots. Current information would be obtained from Jon Postel directly. Later, RFC 790 and then the IANA registry system provided more dynamic and centralized numbering authority.
sections.eli5: This was a snapshot of all the numbers in use on January 1, 1981. The list grew over time and was updated regularly as more protocols and networks came online.

references.text: Feinler, E., and J. Postel, eds., "ARPANET Protocol Handbook", NIC 7104.
